evidence.outcome: Performance for underrepresented darker skin tones given lighter-tone-dominated training data
evidence.effect: Training dataset predominantly lighter skin tones; SkinGPT-4 weaker on darker tones, with 0.10-0.15 differences between lightest and darkest tones.
evidence.quote: Large language models such as SkinGPT-4 showed weaker performance on darker tones.

evidence.title: AI safety evaluation in an underrepresented population: real-world performance of clinical decision support and frontier language models on Medicaid patient messaging triage
evidence.outcome: autonomous triage accuracy in underrepresented Medicaid population
evidence.effect: No configuration met the autonomous benchmark; sensitivity and specificity were 0.594 and 0.592 for best single tool, 0.685 and 0.575 for best ensemble, and 0.297 and 0.874 for cascade.
evidence.quote: No configuration met the autonomous benchmark; sensitivity and specificity reached 0.594 and 0.592 for the best balanced single tool, 0.685 and 0.575 for the best balanced ensemble, and 0.297 and 0.874 for the highest-specificity cascade.

evidence.title: Bias in respiratory diagnoses by Large Language Models (LLMs) in Low-Middle Income Countries (LMICs)
evidence.outcome: Overlap of LLM diagnoses with doctors' diagnoses in LMIC settings versus the UK
evidence.effect: LLMs proposed 32.0% (95% CI 23.1 to 42.3%) of LMIC doctors' diagnoses versus 50% (95% CI 32.6 to 67.4%) in the UK; persisted when country was stated in the prompt (Chi-squared p = 0.028)
evidence.quote: The LLMs proposed fewer of the doctors’ diagnoses in LMICs versus in the UK - 50% (95% CI 32.6 to 67.4%) in the UK compared to 32.0% (95% CI 23.1 to 42.3%) in LMICs.

evidence.title: Uncovering Language Disparity of ChatGPT on Retinal Vascular Disease Classification: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Performance gap across languages and disease categories due to English-centric training
evidence.effect: F1 fell 6.45% with Chinese prompts; VKH and CSC F1 under 4% vs DR/normal above 80%.
evidence.quote: The performance gap between different diseases and prompting strategies demonstrates the potential unfairness brought by the overrepresentation of the major diseases, languages, and countries.

evidence.title: Neuroimaging data repositories and AI-driven healthcare-Global aspirations vs. ethical considerations in machine learning models of neurological disease
evidence.outcome: Change in ML feature importance across simulated datasets with different cohort proportions
evidence.effect: Differing proportions of anosmic and non-anosmic cohorts in bootstrapped datasets (matched, 73% non-anosmic, 76% anosmic) altered key feature importance and even the presence or absence of features.
evidence.quote: We found that the differing proportions of the same cohorts represented in each hypothetical dataset altered not only the relative importance of key features distinguishing between them but even the presence or absence of such features.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (pilot neuroimaging dataset, bootstrapped into simulated datasets of 66-68)

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT and Google Translate for Pediatric Discharge Instruction Translation
evidence.outcome: Potentially clinically significant translation errors (severity score ≤3) for Haitian Creole versus professional translation
evidence.effect: Haitian Creole errors: ChatGPT 33.3% (P < .001), Google Translate 23.3% (P = .024), professional translations 8.3%.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT (33.3%, P < .001) and Google Translate (23.3%, P = .024) contained more potentially clinically significant errors (severity score ≤3) for Haitian Creole than professional translations (8.3%).
evidence.sample_unit: standardized pediatric discharge instructions (each translated into 3 languages by 3 sources)

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Assessment of Pediatric Dental Panoramic Radiographs (DPRs): A Clinical Study
evidence.outcome: AI accuracy detecting caries, fillings, missing teeth in pediatric panoramic radiographs versus adults/general population
evidence.effect: High specificity and accuracy (all above 85%) for caries, fillings and missing teeth, but low precision. Overall accuracy is lower for pediatric patients than for adults or the entire population.
evidence.quote: In conclusion, the overall accuracy of AI algorithms for evaluating permanent dentition in dental panoramic radiographs is lower for pediatric patients than adults or the entire population.

evidence.title: Performance of Machine Learning Suicide Risk Models in an American Indian Population
evidence.outcome: AIAN representation in validation cohorts
evidence.effect: Analytic sample was 94.0% AIAN; VU validation reported no AIAN; MHRN validation had 37 717 of 3 387 741 visits (1.1%) AIAN.
evidence.quote: In comparison, the validation sample for the VU model did not report any American Indian or Alaska Native patients (2080 of 77 973 patients [2.7%] are reported as other race) and reported 85 of 77 973 patients (0.1%) with an attempt included in the analysis.

evidence.title: Performance of Open-Source Large Language Models in Psychiatry: Usability Study Through Comparative Analysis of Non-English Records and English Translations
evidence.outcome: top-1 diagnostic accuracy by input language
evidence.effect: Top-1 accuracy was significantly lower with Korean input compared to English input (59% vs 74.5%, P<.001).
evidence.quote: The model showed significantly higher top-1 diagnostic accuracy with English input (74.5% vs 59%; P<.001), while top-2 accuracy was comparable (89.5% vs 90%; P=.56).

evidence.title: Human evaluators vs. LLM-as-a-Judge: toward scalable evaluation of GenAI in global health
evidence.outcome: Kinyarwanda performance and cost-effectiveness
evidence.effect: Performance and cost-effectiveness fell moving from English to Kinyarwanda; no numeric estimate reported.
evidence.quote: Notably, performance and cost-effectiveness fell when moving from English to Kinyarwanda.

evidence.title: PediatricsMQA: a Multi-modal Pediatrics Question Answering Benchmark
evidence.outcome: LLM/VLM performance on pediatric text and image questions, an underrepresented age group
evidence.effect: Dramatic performance drops in younger cohorts among evaluated open models; age bias described as reflecting pediatric underrepresentation in medical research.
evidence.quote: Evaluating state-of-the-art open models, we find dramatic performance drops in younger cohorts, highlighting the need for age-aware methods to ensure equitable AI support in pediatric care.

evidence.title: The Validity Gap in Health AI Evaluation: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Benchmark Composition
evidence.outcome: Representation of vulnerable populations in benchmark queries
evidence.effect: Pediatrics and older adults each below 11% of the corpus; global health needs neglected.
evidence.quote: Benchmarks also neglected vulnerable populations (pediatrics/older adults <11%) and global health needs.

evidence.title: Assessing equitable use of large language models for clinical decision support in real-world settings: fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia
evidence.outcome: Bias in Global South clinical setting
evidence.effect: Publicly available LLMs predominantly trained in global north settings were biased in a real-world clinical setting.
evidence.quote: Publicly available LLMs, predominantly trained in global north settings, were found to be biased when used in a real-world clinical setting.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for clinical note processing: local fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Performance in Pakistani versus Global North settings
evidence.effect: Models pretrained/fine-tuned on high-income public datasets underperformed in Pakistan, with at least 15% F1 and 35% ROUGE-L/BLEU reductions.
evidence.quote: In conclusion, our findings highlight the underperformance of medical LLMs in a local Pakistani setting compared to those in Global North settings revealing the data-driven biases in existing publicly available medical LLMs, which are predominantly pre-trained on data from high-income settings.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical notes (50 discharge summaries, 150 SOAP notes)

evidence.title: Disparate language and model effects on AI-based translation and recognition of genetic conditions
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Genetic condition identification accuracy across languages, including by language prevalence in training sources
evidence.effect: Significant differences in condition identification by translation method, condition, language, and model; accuracy of some models was more affected by language prevalence, script, and family.
evidence.quote: The accuracy of some models was more affected than others by factors like the conditions' literature prevalence, language script, family, and language prevalence.

evidence.title: Trustworthy AI for radar vital signs: detecting and mitigating gender bias in healthcare
evidence.outcome: Effect of sex representation in training data on model performance
evidence.effect: Male-only data: accuracy 78.2%, RMSE 1.80; female-dominant: accuracy 94.5%, RMSE 0.70. Male-skewed datasets had larger errors and lower success rates.
evidence.quote: These findings reveal a systematic relationship between demographic representation and error magnitude: male-skewed datasets exhibited larger errors and lower success rates, undermining fairness and reliability.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies test representation or remediation of training data, and six report better subgroup performance, but all were offline benchmarks or a survey, and none tested representative validation cohorts or human evaluators in deployment. Health systems can reasonably require representation reporting and subgroup validation from vendors, with the understanding that representation reduced but did not always close performance gaps.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks, and one is a survey experiment. Five benchmarks report gains after adding underrepresented data, while one reports that balanced sex sampling reduced but did not remove gaps. No study measured patient outcomes or ran in live care. Indirectness, unreported populations, and one mixed result lower certainty to very low.

Adult-only segmentation models scored mean Dice below 0.5 for bladder and spleen in children aged 0 to 2, and adding pediatric data raised Dice above 0.85 for all organs. A deployed model showed a 77% false negative rate in an underrepresented subgroup. These results suggest subgroup validation may catch errors before release.

Balanced 50/50 sex sampling narrowed accuracy gaps, yet sampling scenario explained only 0.2% of gap variance, which suggests representation alone may not correct disparities. Synthetic augmentation improved F1 by up to 21% in one benchmark, but no study examined how remediation works within real procurement, retraining, or local validation workflows.

One validation cohort reported no American Indian and Alaska Native patients and another reported 1.1%, although the target sample was 94.0% AIAN. Triage tools missed benchmarks in Medicaid messages, and models performed worse in Korean and Haitian Creole. None of the remediation tests enrolled these populations, so benefit for them remains untested.

FDORA section 3601(b) requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for studies of certain devices, and FDA draft guidance cites this requirement for AI-enabled devices. This obligation covers clinical studies for regulated devices and does not reach many non-device tools such as general-purpose language models used by health systems.

No study reported the cost or staff time of assembling representative data or auditing vendor cohorts. The HEAAL framework states that implementation requires expertise, infrastructure, and personnel effort. Synthetic data pretraining improved fairness across five institutions in one benchmark, which may offer a lower-cost path, but its costs were not measured.

In a survey of 3,000 US respondents, information that a tool used representative US training data increased preference for a visit (AMCE 0.119; 95% CI 0.106 to 0.131). This suggests disclosure of representation may affect patient trust, although stated preference in a vignette may differ from behavior in care.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether representative validation cohorts or representative human evaluators change detection of subgroup errors or patient outcomes in deployment. Prospective studies that compare locally validated and unvalidated tools in live settings, with subgroup results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: Two remediation tests focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies documented failures in Medicaid, safety-net, and non-English settings, so the populations with documented harm are those for which remediation has not been tested.
